summary: This document specifies the preferred method for carrying Delay- and Disruption-Tolerant Networking (DTN) data over the Internet using datagrams. It covers convergence layers for the Bundle Protocol (RFC 5050) and for transporting Licklider Transmission Protocol (LTP) segments (RFC 5326). It is an Experimental specification.

plainLanguage.summary: Some networks are like mail sent by a slow boat with long gaps in service. This explains how to pack that special mail into ordinary Internet packets so it can travel.

questions: what transport for dtn over internet
when to use udp vs dccp for ltp
how large can dtn datagrams be
subtitle: Carrying DTN data over UDP and DCCP instead of TCP.

tldr.problem: DTN protocols need to be tested and deployed over the Internet, but the standard TCP transport is not ideal for all scenarios.
tldr.mechanism: This document specifies how to encapsulate DTN bundles and LTP segments into UDP and DCCP datagrams, with guidance on choosing between them based on congestion control needs.
tldr.outcome: DCCP is recommended for internet transport of LTP; UDP is acceptable only on local networks or with explicit congestion control. The document is Experimental.

today: RFC 7122 is an Experimental specification published in March 2014. It provides practical guidance for DTN deployment over the Internet and has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Introduction to DTN Transport
sections.content:
Delay- and Disruption-Tolerant Networking (DTN) protocols, particularly the Bundle Protocol and the Licklider Transmission Protocol (LTP), are designed to handle communications over networks with long delays, intermittent connectivity, or high error rates. While these protocols can operate over any underlying transport, it is often desirable to test and deploy them over standard Internet links.

This document specifies how to carry DTN protocols over datagrams—specifically UDP and DCCP—rather than the traditional TCP Convergence Layer. The choice of transport matters because DTN protocols and TCP have different reliability models, and using the wrong one can waste bandwidth or violate Internet congestion control requirements.
sections.plainLanguage: DTN is for networks that have big gaps in service. The internet is always on, so you need special instructions for moving DTN mail through regular internet pipes.

sections.title: Why Choose DCCP Over UDP
sections.content:
Both UDP and DCCP are datagram protocols that avoid the overhead and reliability guarantees of TCP. However, they differ significantly in one critical way: congestion control.

The Bundle Protocol and LTP both provide their own reliability mechanisms, so running them over TCP would be redundant. UDP offers no reliability and no congestion control—which is a serious problem on the public Internet. DCCP (Datagram Congestion Control Protocol) was designed specifically for this scenario: it provides congestion control without retransmission.

The specification RECOMMENDS DCCP for transporting LTP segments across the Internet whenever possible. UDP can be used only on isolated local networks or in cases where the DTN implementation explicitly provides congestion control consistent with RFC 5405. Any DTN implementation that permits UDP to carry non-trivial amounts of data outside an isolated network MUST implement congestion control.
sections.plainLanguage: The Internet depends on everybody playing fair and slowing down when traffic is heavy. UDP never slows down, which is bad. DCCP has a way to slow down fairly, making it safe for the Internet.

sections.title: Fragmentation and Datagram Size
sections.content:
Bundles can be arbitrarily large, but a single UDP or DCCP datagram is limited to around 64 KB in IPv4. More importantly, large datagrams that must be fragmented at the IP layer incur enormous efficiency penalties.

To avoid IP-layer fragmentation, the Bundle Protocol's own fragmentation mechanism SHOULD be used to create fragments small enough to fit in a single datagram that matches the network's Path MTU (Maximum Transmission Unit). Implementations can use IP Path MTU Discovery (RFC 1191 for IPv4, RFC 1981 for IPv6) to determine the MTU, or the newer RFC 4821 approach that does not rely on ICMP Packet Too Big messages.

For DCCP, implementations MUST NOT accept data segments that cannot fit in a single MTU-sized datagram, since DCCP does not support IP fragmentation by default. For UDP, implementations SHOULD avoid creating segments that require IP fragmentation.
sections.plainLanguage: Huge packets break apart and get reassembled, wasting time and space. So split them into medium-sized packets that fit through the network in one piece.

sections.title: Bundle Protocol and LTP Over Datagrams
sections.content:
When using datagrams as the convergence layer for the Bundle Protocol, every datagram MUST contain exactly one bundle or a keep-alive message (4 octets of zeros). Bundles too large for the path MTU SHOULD be fragmented at the Bundle Protocol layer to prevent IP fragmentation.

For LTP, the datagram layer serves as the point-to-point transport. LTP segments are likewise sent one per datagram. LTP already provides acknowledgement and retransmission, making it a natural fit for unreliable datagram transports. LTP MUST perform its own segmentation to ensure every segment fits in a single packet without IP fragmentation.

The specification assigns specific port numbers: port 4556 for Bundle Protocol over UDP or DCCP, and port 1113 for LTP over UDP or DCCP. DCCP also uses service codes (7107696 for LTP, 1685351985 for Bundle Protocol). Keep-alive datagrams MAY be sent during idle periods (using 4 octets of zeros) with a configurable interval that SHOULD default to 15 seconds and MUST NOT be shorter than 15 seconds. These keep-alives help refresh state in firewalls and NAT devices.
sections.plainLanguage: Pack one bundle per packet. LTP segments go one per packet too. That way everything fits nicely without breaking apart.

sections.title: Checksums and Security
sections.content:
Both the Bundle Protocol and LTP assume they are transmitting over an erasure channel—a channel that either delivers packets correctly or not at all. This assumption means they do not protect against corruption.

For DCCP, implementations MUST set the Checksum Coverage to zero to ensure the entire packet is checksummed, and receivers MUST ignore packets with partial checksum coverage. For UDP, implementations MUST NOT disable UDP checksums on the transmitter side, and receivers MUST NOT disable checksum validation. Even with UDP checksums enabled, a small probability of undetected corruption remains, so implementations SHOULD use optional security extensions available in the Bundle Protocol or LTP to protect against message corruption.

Hosts MAY use IP address filtering to limit the origin of data to known sources, reducing the risk of denial-of-service attacks where a malicious host floods the receiving host with packets. Hosts SHOULD use authentication methods available in the DTN specifications to prevent unknown sources from inserting forged data.
sections.plainLanguage: Turn on the checksum to catch broken packets. It is not perfect, so important data should use extra protection built into the DTN protocols themselves.
